National Consumer Disputes Redressal
Ajay Kumar Gupta vs Prateek Infra Projects India Pvt. Ltd. on 31 August, 2023
NATIONAL CONSUMER DISPUTES REDRESSAL COMMISSION NEW DELHI   CONSUMER CASE NO. 2219 OF 2018 1. AJAY KUMAR GUPTA R/o C-25, NIZAMUDDIN EAST, NEW DELHI - 110013 ...........Complainant(s) Versus   1. PRATEEK INFRA PROJECTS INDIA PVT. LTD. R/o G-50, LGF, LAJPAT NAGAR-II, NEW DELHI - 110024 ...........Opp.Party(s) 
 BEFORE:     HON'BLE MR. SUBHASH CHANDRA,PRESIDING MEMBER 
 FOR THE COMPLAINANT : MR PRABHAKAR TIWARI, ADVOCATE WITH
 MR S M ANSARI, ADVOCATE FOR THE OPP. PARTY : MR SUDEEP SINGH, ADVOCATE WITH
 MR AMIT MALIK, ADVOCATES 
 Dated : 31 August 2023 ORDER 

1.
This consumer complaint under section 21(a)(i) read with 12(1)(a)  of the
Consumer Protection Act, 1986
(in short, the 'Act') is filed against the opposite party alleging deficiency in not handing over possession of the flat booked by the complainants within the promised time and seeking refund of the amount deposited with interest as compensation and other costs.
2.      The complainant states that he booked flat G-2315, 22nd Floor, Tower G, 'Prateek Edifice', Sector 107, Gautam Budh Nagar on transfer from the original allottee, M/s DGAS Promoters Pvt. Ltd, which was approved by the opposite party, for a sale consideration of Rs 1,30,88,600/- based on Allotment Letter-cum-Apartment Buyers' Agreement (in short, 'the Agreement') dated 25.11.2012. This Agreement mentioned the date of possession as December, 2016 in clause 43. The same terms were to apply to the complainant according to the opposite party as he stepped into the shoes of the original allotee. Complainant paid Rs 1,33,61,149/- or 95%. However, opposite party sought execution of a fresh Allotment Letter-cum-Apartment Buyers' Agreement which had different and one-sided terms including date of possession and revision of purchase price from Rs 6,750/- per sq ft to Rs 7,500/- per sq ft. The complainant states he was compelled to sign this document on 21.10.2016 as he had no alternative having paid a substantial amount. Receipt for Rs 4,26,342/- was not provided and the date of possession was extended arbitrarily to June 2017 with grace period of 5 months. An offer of possession was made on 01.08.2018 but no Occupancy Certificate was made available though requested for. A visit to the site revealed that construction work was underway and facilities such as lifts and common facilities were not in place. Opposite party also raised a demand of Rs.31,319/- as 'Farmers Compensation' and Rs 10,000/- for 'Fiber to Home Deposit'. No response was provided to the complainant's legal notice dated 23.08.2018 by the opposite party and hence this complaint has been filed as per the pecuniary jurisdiction of this Commission and since the complainant falls under
section 2(i)(d)
as a 'consumer' and also since there is a continuing cause of action under the Agreement dated 21.10.2016. The complainant's prayer is to direct the opposite party to:
(a) hand over possession complete in all respects expeditiously;
(b)    pay compensation for delayed possession @ 18% p.a. from the original date of promised delivery till the actual date of possession;
(c)    provide all infrastructural facilities of road, water, electricity, sewerage with necessary governmental clearances;
(d)    provide fully operational common amenities and facilities including club house, swimming pool, etc as per the project prospectus;
(e)    provide for a third party audit to correctly measure the super area and built-up area and ascertain conformance of project quality in accordance with promised specifications;
(f)     pay the differential amount to the complainant based on the area determined along with 18% interest compounded quarterly from the date of booking till the date of payment;
(g)    charge maintenance from the date of handing over of possession;

 

Or, in the alternative,
refund the amount of Rs 1,33,61,149/- with interest @ 18% from the respective dates of deposit till realization; and
(h)    refrain from giving effect to unfair clauses unilaterally incorporated in the Allotment Letter;
(i)     pay Rs 5,00,000/- towards compensation for financial loss, harassment and mental agony;
(j)     pay Rs 1,00,000/- towards cost of litigation;

 

(k)    pass any other order as deemed fit and proper.
3.      The opposite party resisted the complaint by way of a written statement and denied all allegations. It was stated that the delay beyond June 2017 with 5 months of grace period was subject to force majeure conditions as per clauses 43 and 48 of the agreement dated 21.10.2016. In the instant case the delay was due to the orders of the NOIDA and due to Writ Petitions filed before the Allahabad High Court relating to land acquisition issues which were quashed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court decided WP (Civil) No. 33341/2014 on 11.07.2016. Occupancy Certificate had been issued on 20.07.2018 for towers D, E and F on 29.10.2018. According to the opposite party, applicability of the force majeure clause automatically extends the period of construction to cover the period during which it applies as per clause 51 and, therefore, there was no delay. It is contended that the agreement provides for compensation for delay @ Rs 5/- per sq ft per month for the super area and therefore, the claim of 18% interest does not apply. The offer of possession according to the opposite party was dated 01.08.2018 with fit out period of 90 days and a revised demand issued on 06.08.2018 followed by reminders dated 19.08.2018 and 18.10.2018 which was not complied with by the complainant.
4.     Opposite party contends the complainant is not maintainable on ground of pecuniary jurisdiction since an offer of possession has been made and therefore, the alternative relief of refund also does not lie. The complainant is stated to be a defaulter who has not paid the final instalment and so he cannot seek the reliefs sought. All facilities and amenities having been provided; these reliefs do not lie. It is contended that there is no dispute with regard to the super area; hence, this prayer is a request for a roving enquiry which is baseless. It is argued that the complaint of deficiency in service also does not lie as the delay was due to force majeure causes not attributable to the opposite party. The disputes raised are necessarily arbitrable and cannot be decided in summary jurisdiction of the Commission and therefore, the complaint is not maintainable in view of the clause for arbitration in the agreement.
5.      Parties led their evidence on affidavit and filed the rejoinder, written submission and short synopsis of arguments. I have heard the learned counsel for both the sides and perused the evidence on record carefully.
6.      During arguments the learned counsel pressed for the alternative prayer for refund of the money deposited along with interest, compensation and cost of litigation. The counsel for the complainant argued that the opposite party had been deficient in services and was guilty of unfair trade practice since the agreement was arbitrarily revised through one-sided clauses which he was unable to resist having paid a considerable amount of money. The date of handing over was changed arbitrarily and recourse was being taken to force majeure reasons which the opposite party should have been aware of as they dated to 2014. Reliance is placed by the complainant on the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
Wg Cdr Arifur Rahman Khan & Aleya Sultana & Ors. Vs. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd.
, (2020) 16,SCC 512;
Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. Vs. Govindan Raghavan
, (2019) 5 SCC 725;
R.V. Prasannakumar Vs. Mantri Castles (P) Ltd.
, (2020) 14 SCC 769;
Ghaziabad Development Authority Vs. Balbir Singh
, (
2004) 5 SCC 65 and DLF Homes Panchkula (P) Ltd. Vs. D.S. Dhanda
, (2020) 16 SCC 318.
Reliance is also placed on this Commission's judgment in
Geetu Gidwani Verma Vs. Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd.
, 2018 SCC OnLine NCDRC 1164.
7.      On behalf of the opposite party it was admitted that there had been a delay in the completion of the project. However, reliance was placed on clause 53 of the Agreement for the applicability of force majeure conditions as per clauses 43 and 48 to justify the delay. Apart from the preliminary objections, on merits it was argued that the Occupancy Certificate was available for the concerned tower and that offer of possession had been made which, though 8 months late, was not unreasonable and that the complainant is bound to take possession of the flat and that the prayer for possession with interest was not sustainable. It is contended that time was not of the essence in the agreement. Reliance was placed on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
Ireo Grace Realtech Private Ltd. Vs. Abhishek Khanna & Ors.
, 2021 (3) SCC 241; M/s Hind Construction Contractors by its
Sole Proprietor Bhikam Chand Mulchand Jain (Dead) by LRs Vs. State of Maharashtra
in CA Nos. 483 and 1769 of 1969, (1979) 2 SCC 70 decided on 30.01.1979 and this Commission's judgment in Prateek Garg & Anr. Vs. M/s Prateek Infraprojects India Pvt. Ltd., CC No. 694 of 2018 dated 03.11.2022 relating to the same project.
8.      The preliminary issues raised by the opposite party have been considered. The settled law on pecuniary jurisdiction as held by this Commission in
Ambarish Kumar Shukla and 21 Ors vs Ferrous Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., I
2017 CPJ 1 (NC) and Renu Singh vs Experion Developers Pvt. Ltd., CC no.1703 of 2018 is that the principle for determining the pecuniary jurisdiction is the total consideration paid by the complainant or persons who have joined the complaint in a joint complaint and other damages claimed to determine such jurisdiction. In view of this position of law the contention of the opposite party regarding pecuniary jurisdiction does not sustain. The opposite party's contention that in view of the provision of a clause for arbitration in the Agreement, this complaint does not lie before this Commission has been considered.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in its judgment in
Emaar MGF Land Ltd. Vs. Aftab Singh
,  (2019) 12 SCC 751 that the proceedings under the
Consumer Protection Act, 1986
are not restrained by the existence of an arbitration clause since the remedy under the Act is in addition to other provisions under the law.
It has also reiterated this view in M/s
Imperia Structures Ltd. Vs. Anil Patni & Anr.
, (2020) 10 SCC 783 decided on 02.11.2010 that "remedies under the
Consumer Protection Act
were in addition to the remedies available under special statutes (and) the provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of any other law for the time being in force". Hence, this argument cannot be sustained.
As for the contention of the opposite party that the complainant is not entitled to claim interest for the delay in possession, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has
laid down in
Pioneer Urban land and
Infrastructure Ltd. Vs. Govindan Raghavan
, (2019) 5 SCC 725 in Civil Appeal no. 12238 of 2018 decided on 02.04.2019 that an allottee as a consumer is entitled to seek refund of the money paid by him to the opposite party/builder in case of inordinate delay on the part of the opposite party to hand over possession.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court has also held in
Kolkata West International City Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Devasis Rudra, Civil Appeal No.
3182 of 2019 decided on 25.03.2019 that "It would be manifestly unreasonable to construe the contract between the parties as requiring the buyer to wait indefinitely for possession". In the present case, the delay is of nearly 8 months. However, considering that the amount paid is substantial, seeking compensation for delay is not unwarranted.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in
Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. Vs. Geetu Gidwani Verma & Anr., Civil Appeal No.
12238 of 2018 with No. 1677 of 2019 dated 02.04.2019 laid down that a buyer cannot be compelled to take possession of a flat when there is delay in delivery of possession by the builder and the buyer is entitled to refund along with compensation/interest for such delay.
9.      On merits, the contention of the opposite party that there was no deficiency in service has been considered. Admittedly, the occupancy certificate obtained is dated 20.07.2018 and the offer of possession is dated 01.08.2018. The revised agreement dated 21.10.2016 stipulated the promised date of possession as June 2017 with a grace period of 5 months, i.e., November 2017. The opposite party's argument that in view of the orders of the Allahabad High Court in Writ Petitions relating to land issues, force majeure conditions are applicable needs to be considered in light of the averment of the complainant that the opposite party would have been aware of these issues in 2016 at the time of the revised agreement since the WPs dated to 2014. There is merit in this argument. The opposite party has not produced any document to prove that it kept the complainant abreast of the legal impediments in the project. Instead, it kept demanding and receiving deposits during this period. It also did not penalize the complainant for the default in payment of the last instalment. Therefore, its argument that there was no deficiency in service or the complainant is not entitled to seek refund cannot be accepted.
10.    From the material on record and the arguments advanced by both the learned counsel for the parties, it is manifest that the opposite party revised the Allotment Letter-cum-Apartment Buyers' Agreement after permitting the complainant to step into the shoes of the original allottee. The basic rate of construction of the flat was revised upwardly and the date of possession was revised. Even though there was a grace period of 5 months for construction, the opposite party has now claimed shelter under clause 53 of the agreement. The opposite party submits that there were a series of litigations regarding the land acquisition notifications by NOIDA which finally came to be vacated in 2016. However, it is also stated that the NOIDA acted in confusion since the project lands in Sector 107 related to another village and were not covered by the stay but which caused the opposite party to slow down the pace of construction. This argument cannot be accepted to justify the delay in view of opposite party having admitted that the lands of the opposite party for the project were not specifically covered by any notifications which were quashed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court or that they were covered in the dispute before the Allahabad High Court. The justification for the applicability of force majeure conditions on this reasoning, therefore, does not hold ground.
The opposite party cannot insist that the complainant accept possession of the flat especially since there has been a delay on the part of the opposite party. The complainant has undisputedly paid nearly 95% of the sale consideration. His exercising the option to seek a refund with interest cannot be faulted. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in
Experion Developers Pvt. Ltd Vs. Sushma Ashok Shiroor, Civil Appeal No.
6044 of 2019 decided on 07.04.2022 that " ... interest payable on the amount deposited to be restitutionary and also compensatory, interest has to be from the date of deposit of the amounts" and following the decision in
DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. Vs. DS Dhanda
, that "... the interest on the refund shall be payable from the dates of deposit".  An interest rate of 18%, however, would be inequitable, especially since there is an offer of possession. Accordingly, a 9% p.a. simple interest rate is considered to be appropriate.
9.      For the aforementioned reasons, the complaint is found to have merits and is liable to succeed. It is accordingly allowed in part with the following directions:
(i)     opposite party is directed to refund the entire amount of Rs 1,33,61,149/- with 9% interest from the respective dates of deposit;
(ii)    this order shall be complied within 8 weeks of this order failing which the rate of interest shall be 12% per annum till realization;
(iii)    Opposite party shall also pay Rs 50,000/- to the complainant as cost of litigation.
All pending IAs stand disposed of with this order.
...................................... SUBHASH CHANDRA PRESIDING MEMBER
